vignette:
Mark, a 54-year-old civil servant, had always been a reliable presence in his community, known for his dedication to public service. However, beneath his composed exterior lay the scars of a traumatic past. Years earlier, he had endured a harrowing experience of physical abuse at the hands of a former romantic partner. This trauma had left him grappling with a profound sense of loss of control that reverberated through his everyday life. Even now, the memory of that violence would surface unexpectedly, often triggered by seemingly innocuous situations-like being alone in a room or encountering men who reminded him of his abuser. When these triggers emerged, Mark felt an urgent need to fill his time with activities or socializing afterward, as solitude became a frightening prospect that could invite the very memories he dreaded. When these memories would come rushing back, Mark felt an urgent need to fill his time with activities or socializing afterward, as the weight of those memories made solitude feel unbearable. Each time a memory surfaced, he instinctively sought out the company of others, believing that if he kept himself busy, he could stave off the haunting thoughts that lingered in the silence. When these memories surfaced, Mark felt an overwhelming compulsion to fill his time with activities or socializing afterward, fearing that being alone would allow those haunting thoughts to consume him. When he found himself sleeping alone, the sensation of vulnerability would wash over him, making it impossible to shake the feeling that he was once again powerless and at risk.

To cope with these triggers, Mark had developed several maladaptive strategies. He would often keep himself constantly surrounded by people, filling his social calendar to the brim, as if the noise and bustle could drown out the haunting echoes of his past. This need to avoid moments of solitude stemmed from the terrifying memories that lurked just beneath the surface. Each time Mark was reminded of the abuse, he felt an urgency to fill his time with activities and socializing, as if keeping busy could shield him from the memories that threatened to overwhelm him. He had come to believe that if he were alone, the memories would crash in on him like a tidal wave, overwhelming his thoughts and emotions. The constant need to avoid moments of solitude only heightened the frequency of triggers, as the memories would often return with renewed intensity in the presence of reminders he had hoped to escape. Yet, despite his efforts to stay busy, the memories would still find their way back to him. The more he tried to keep himself distracted, the more vivid and intrusive these memories became, as if his attempts at avoidance only fueled their return. He had come to realize that by constantly filling his schedule, he was merely postponing the inevitable confrontation with those memories, which only seemed to grow stronger and more insistent during the moments he tried to push them away. Each time he filled his schedule to the brim or surrounded himself with others, it seemed to reinforce the memories, making them more potent and inescapable whenever they surfaced. After the memory would surface, even innocuous moments-a sudden noise or an unexpected greeting-would feel like warnings, igniting his anxiety as he braced for something to go wrong. The taste of blood from that fateful night would suddenly flood his senses, overwhelming him with vivid recollections that felt so real, it was as if he were reliving the trauma all over again. 

Mark found it hard to recall the details of the abuse when he tried to deliberately remember, often drawing a blank. Yet, whenever the memories did break through, they hit him with such force that even the most mundane reminders would leave him scrambling to avoid any situation that could bring them back. The powerful nature of these memories served as relentless triggers, igniting a wave of anxiety that pushed him further into his avoidance strategies. This difficulty in accessing his memories frustrated him, but it also reassured him. After all, if he couldn't remember the specifics, perhaps the pain could remain buried. Yet, the more he avoided these memories, the more potent the triggers became. He would often experience flashes of terror, sending him spiraling back into a state of hyper-vigilance whenever he was confronted with reminders of his trauma. It was as if the memories, once triggered, would awaken a surge of panic that he couldn't escape, making him hyper-aware of every potential reminder around him. Mark's constant avoidance of solitude and social events had created an environment where every reminder, no matter how small, became a trigger, amplifying his sense of danger and keeping him on edge. The mere presence of men in close proximity would elicit an intense response, priming him for a fight-or-flight reaction, even when there was no real threat present.

Mark's maladaptive strategies created a cycle that seemed inescapable. The more he surrounded himself with others to avoid being alone, the more he found that his memories would intrude upon his thoughts at the most inconvenient times, often triggered by the very situations he tried to evade. This avoidance had created a cycle where every effort to keep busy and surround himself with people only amplified the frequency of his triggers, each social gathering turning into a minefield of potential reminders that left him feeling even more vulnerable. He had started to feel trapped, knowing that his strategies to cope were themselves becoming barriers to healing. The more he distanced himself from confronting the memories through these strategies, the more vivid and intrusive the memories became, clinging to him in a way he couldn't escape. His constant avoidance had paradoxically kept these memories fresh, ensuring that when they did surface, they emerged with a force that felt insurmountable, as if all his efforts to suppress them had only intensified their presence. His attempts to keep busy and avoid introspection had paradoxically kept the trauma fresh, ensuring that when he did confront those memories, they would emerge with a force that felt insurmountable. His avoidance had paradoxically kept the memories fresh, ensuring that whenever he tried to suppress them, they only emerged with greater intensity and urgency. The vividness of his memories clashed with his desire to forget, leading to a frustrating conflict where avoidance only seemed to strengthen the hold of his trauma on his life.

Now, after years of living in this painful cycle, Mark sought help. He had come to realize that the consequences of his trauma were seeping into every aspect of his life, straining his relationship and affecting his work. He feared that if he didn't confront these demons soon, he would lose everything he held dear. Sitting in the therapist's office, he felt a flicker of hope mixed with a paralyzing fear of what facing his memories might entail. Would he be able to reclaim the control he had lost so long ago? Mark was uncertain, but he knew that he could no longer allow the past to dictate his future.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not convey how triggers influence the development of maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not convey how memories influence the triggers experienced by Mark.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."

  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."

  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Mark, a 54-year-old civil servant, had always been a reliable presence in his community, known for his dedication to public service. However, beneath his composed exterior lay the scars of a traumatic past. Years earlier, he had endured a harrowing experience of physical abuse at the hands of a former romantic partner. This trauma had left him grappling with a profound sense of loss of control that reverberated through his everyday life. Even now, the memory of that violence would surface unexpectedly, often triggered by seemingly innocuous situations—like being alone in a room or encountering men who reminded him of his abuser. When these memories would come rushing back, Mark felt an urgent need to fill his time with activities or socializing afterward, as the weight of those memories made solitude feel unbearable. Each time a memory surfaced, he instinctively sought out the company of others, believing that if he kept himself busy, he could stave off the haunting thoughts that lingered in the silence. When these memories surfaced, Mark felt an overwhelming compulsion to fill his time with activities or socializing afterward, fearing that being alone would allow those haunting thoughts to consume him. When he found himself sleeping alone, the sensation of vulnerability would wash over him, making it impossible to shake the feeling that he was once again powerless and at risk.

To cope with these triggers, Mark had developed several maladaptive strategies. He would often keep himself constantly surrounded by people, filling his social calendar to the brim, as if the noise and bustle could drown out the haunting echoes of his past. This need to avoid moments of solitude stemmed from the terrifying memories that lurked just beneath the surface. Each time Mark was reminded of the abuse, he felt an urgency to fill his time with activities and socializing, as if keeping busy could shield him from the memories that threatened to overwhelm him. He had come to believe that if he were alone, the memories would crash in on him like a tidal wave, overwhelming his thoughts and emotions. The constant need to avoid moments of solitude only heightened the frequency of triggers, as the memories would often return with renewed intensity in the presence of reminders he had hoped to escape. Yet, despite his efforts to stay busy, the memories would still find their way back to him. The more he tried to keep himself distracted, the more vivid and intrusive these memories became, as if his attempts at avoidance only fueled their return. He had come to realize that by constantly filling his schedule, he was merely postponing the inevitable confrontation with those memories, which only seemed to grow stronger and more insistent during the moments he tried to push them away. Each time he filled his schedule to the brim or surrounded himself with others, it seemed to reinforce the memories, making them more potent and inescapable whenever they surfaced. After the memory would surface, even innocuous moments—a sudden noise or an unexpected greeting—would feel like warnings, igniting his anxiety as he braced for something to go wrong. The taste of blood from that fateful night would suddenly flood his senses, overwhelming him with vivid recollections that felt so real, it was as if he were reliving the trauma all over again. 

Mark found it hard to recall the details of the abuse when he tried to deliberately remember, often drawing a blank. Yet, whenever the memories did break through, they hit him with such force that even the most mundane reminders would leave him scrambling to avoid any situation that could bring them back. This difficulty in accessing his memories frustrated him, but it also reassured him. After all, if he couldn’t remember the specifics, perhaps the pain could remain buried. Yet, the more he avoided these memories, the more potent the triggers became. He would often experience flashes of terror, sending him spiraling back into a state of hyper-vigilance whenever he was confronted with reminders of his trauma. It was as if the memories, once triggered, would awaken a surge of panic that he couldn’t escape, making him hyper-aware of every potential reminder around him. Mark’s constant avoidance of solitude and social events had created an environment where every reminder, no matter how small, became a trigger, amplifying his sense of danger and keeping him on edge. The mere presence of men in close proximity would elicit an intense response, priming him for a fight-or-flight reaction, even when there was no real threat present.

Mark’s maladaptive strategies created a cycle that seemed inescapable. The more he surrounded himself with others to avoid being alone, the more he found that his memories would intrude upon his thoughts at the most inconvenient times, often triggered by the very situations he tried to evade. He had started to feel trapped, knowing that his strategies to cope were themselves becoming barriers to healing. The more he distanced himself from confronting the memories through these strategies, the more vivid and intrusive the memories became, clinging to him in a way he couldn't escape. His attempts to keep busy and avoid introspection had paradoxically kept the trauma fresh, ensuring that when he did confront those memories, they would emerge with a force that felt insurmountable. His avoidance had paradoxically kept the memories fresh, ensuring that whenever he tried to suppress them, they only emerged with greater intensity and urgency. The vividness of his memories clashed with his desire to forget, leading to a frustrating conflict where avoidance only seemed to strengthen the hold of his trauma on his life.

Now, after years of living in this painful cycle, Mark sought help. He had come to realize that the consequences of his trauma were seeping into every aspect of his life, straining his relationship and affecting his work. He feared that if he didn’t confront these demons soon, he would lose everything he held dear. Sitting in the therapist's office, he felt a flicker of hope mixed with a paralyzing fear of what facing his memories might entail. Would he be able to reclaim the control he had lost so long ago? Mark was uncertain, but he knew that he could no longer allow the past to dictate his future.
